المشاهد الصعبة جداً في نيبال وهنا وثقنا مشاهد زي ما احنا شايفينها لحظة رعب أو لحظة وقوع انهيار أرضي ضخم وتساقط أتربة زي ما احنا شايفين وصخور وردم أجزاء من مجرى نهر تشورلاني غربي نيبال وده وسط تحذيرات من احتمال انسداد النهر ووقوع فيضانات أكبر وزي ما احنا شايفين من خلال تغطيتنا الإخبارية من الوطن لايف لهذه الكارثة الصعبة في نيبال تسببت أو تسبب انهيار أرضي ضخم في إقليم دراشولا غربي نيبال بإغلاق جزئي لمجرى نهر تشورلاني تشاميليا وسط تحذيرات رسمية كمان من فيضانات جديدة ومفاجئة وكانت تسببت الأمطار المتواصلة وأدت إلى تساقط كتل هائلة من الأتربة زي ما احنا شايفين والصخور تم إجلاء نحو 30 شخص من السكان القريبين إلى مناطق آمنة مع استمرار تحذيرات السلطات بعدم الاقتراب من ضفاف النهر وخليني أقول لحضراتكم آخر التفاصيل لهذه الكارثة وهنا أعلن الناطق باسم الجيش النيبالي راجا رام باستين اللي ده السبت استمرار عمليات البحث والإنقاذ عن ناجين محتملين عالقين داخل أنفاق في شمال البلاد وذلك طبعا بعد العثور امبارح على عاملين كمان كانوا محاصرين داخل أحد الأنفاق منذ الفيضانات المدمرة اللي اجتاحت المنطقة زي ما قلنا في 26 أغسطس الماضي قال باسينيت إن فرق الإنقاذ بتواصل جهودها داخل الأنفاق مؤكدا عدم ورود معلومات جديدة بشأن مصير العالقين مع استمرار عمليات البحث وعلى فكرة يأتي نجاح فرق الإنقاذ يعني نجاحهم في انتشال اثنين من العمال النيباليين هما سانجاي ساها البالغ من العمر 30 سنة وكبير مهرجان 45 عام من نفق في موقع كمان بناء سد ريشولي اللي هو إي ثلاثة وذلك بعد بقائهم محاصرين داخل النفق ده لمدة تسع أيام والتفاصيل كمان بتقول إن انتشلت السلطات النيبالية شخصين على قيد الحياة من نفق لتوليد الطاقة الكهرومائية الكهرومائية في نيبال بعد تسع أيام من فيضانات مفاجئة مميتة جدا دفنت المشاريع في الطين العميق وتركتهم محاصرين تم إنقاذ العمال الحمد لله خلال عملية في نفق تريشولي وده مشروع على فكرة للطاقة الكهرومائية في أحد المناطق الأكثر تضررا من فيضانات الأسبوع الماضي وده وفقا لما ذكره المتحدث باسم الجيش النيبالي راجارام علما على فكرة تمت يعني أو دمرت معظم مشاريع الطاقة الكهرومائية على طول نهر بوتشيكي وتدفقت موجة من المية والحطام والطين إلى أسفل الوادي الأسبوع الماضي كمان نتيجة لانهيارات جليدي أو انهيار جليدي ذائب على الحدود بين نيبال والتبت اللي تسبب أو تسيطر عليه الصين أفادت وكالة إدارة الكوارث في نيبال بمقتل ما لا يقل عن أكثر من 1287 شخص في الفيضانات على فكرة لا يزال أكثر من 5000 وأكثر من شخص في عداد المفقودين. يعني خليني أقولكم إنه عدد القتلى وصل لأكثر من 1287. عدد المفقودين تجاوز أكثر من 5087 مفقود وسط عمليات بحث مستمرة. الخسائر المادية على فكرة قدرت بنحو 2.56 مليار دولار. يعني أكثر من 387 مليار روبية نيبالية. دمرت الفيضانات آلاف المنازل. ألحقت أضرار كبيرة. تواصل فرق الإنقاذ النيبالية دلوقتي عمليات البحث عن المفقودين. وده على فكرة في يعني صعوبات كبيرة بتواجههم للوصول للمناطق الأكثر تضرراً بسبب الدمار الهائل اللي إحنا شايفينه واللي لحق بالطرق والجسور والبنية التحتية. الكارثة دي بدأت في 26 أغسطس. زي ما قلنا تسببت إنهيارات واسعة في تدفقات مائية وطينية مدمرة زي ما إحنا شايفين. إجتاحت مناطق في نيبال مخلفة أعداد كبيرة من الضحايا والمفقودين ودمار واسع في المنازل والطرق والمنشآت. هنتابع مع حضراتكم كل التفاصيل من خلال تغطيتنا الإخبارية من غرفة الأخبار والوطن لايف معي أنا هبة

uKZabjdMj2E.transcript: Un gigantesco deslizamiento de tierra sepultó varias viviendas en China, un tornado afectó a Francia, inundaciones tienen en emergencia a Bélgica y los rescates contrarreloj en Texas marcan una nueva jornada de emergencias en el planeta. El pánico se desató en segundos. Los habitantes del distrito de Pengshui en el suroccidente de China huían mientras a sus espaldas un deslizamiento de tierra levantaba una enorme nube de polvo. Más de 10 edificios, entre ellos varios residenciales, quedaron sepultados. 1,100 personas fueron evacuadas mientras cientos de rescatistas buscan a quienes podrían haber quedado atrapados. Entre tanto en Francia, en medio de una ola de calor sin precedentes, un tornado azotó localidades al norte de Saint-Étienne en el oriente del país. El fenómeno arrancó techos y derribó árboles mientras el granizo rompió ventanas y el temporal dejó miles de hogares sin electricidad. La intensidad y el tamaño del granizo fueron bastante sorprendentes. Nunca había visto nada igual. Granizo más grande que pelotas de golf. En Bélgica, las lluvias torrenciales provocaron inundaciones en la provincia de Namur. Calles, viviendas y comercios quedaron bajo el agua. Una vez se dieron las inundaciones, los residentes comenzaron labores de limpieza. Fue catastrófico, fue un desastre. Estábamos paralizados porque al final no había nada más que pudiéramos hacer. Solo nos quedaba esperar a que pasara. En Texas, las inundaciones volvieron a desatar una carrera contra el tiempo. En el condado de Uvalde, una familia y su perrito fueron rescatados en helicóptero tras quedar aislados por el agua. Hasta el momento se han reportado dos personas muertas y más de 230 rescatadas. El gobernador declaró 59 condados del centro y sur del estado como zonas de desastre mientras se mantienen las alertas por el riesgo de nuevas crecidas de los ríos.

wYIQccfKhsU.title: 🔴 NEPAL: ALERTA POR UN NUEVO DESLIZAMIENTO
wYIQccfKhsU.description:
La catástrofe ocurrida en Nepal, donde el derrumbe de un glaciar provocó una inundación repentina con al menos 1.300 muertos y 5.000 desaparecidos, ha puesto en alerta a comunidades de todo el mundo sobre los riesgos asociados al cambio climático. El fenómeno, vinculado al calentamiento global, acelera la fractura y derretimiento de glaciares, generando peligrosas avalanchas de agua y hielo que pueden arrasar ciudades enteras en cuestión de segundos.

En la Patagonia argentina, especialmente en El Chaltén (Santa Cruz), autoridades locales junto a vecinos y organismos como Parques Nacionales están implementando planes de contingencia para anticipar posibles emergencias similares. Se monitorea particularmente el glaciar cercano a la Laguna Torre y al cerro Solo, cuya ladera inestable podría desencadenar una inundación repentina si se produjera un desprendimiento masivo. mcFa1ZWc7SM.title: Palos Verdes Landslide: $54 Million to Buy and Demolish Luxury Homes
mcFa1ZWc7SM.description:
#California #PalosVerdes #Landslide

Million-dollar homes, breathtaking ocean views, and a hillside that refuses to stop moving. The Palos Verdes landslide is turning one of Southern California’s most desirable coastal communities into a devastating real estate nightmare.

In Rancho Palos Verdes, the Portuguese Bend landslide complex stretches across approximately 680 acres. Luxury homes are cracking, roads are buckling, and underground utility lines are being damaged as the land continues shifting toward the Pacific Ocean.

Hundreds of households have experienced utility disruptions, while some homeowners have been forced to abandon properties they spent decades building and paying for. Now, FEMA has awarded more than $54 million in grants to support property buyouts and demolition.

Despite extensive groundwater pumping, emergency repairs, and millions of dollars in mitigation efforts, the Palos Verdes landslide continues to threaten homes and critical infrastructure.

In this video, we explore the geological history behind the disaster, the impact of atmospheric river storms, the growing financial burden on homeowners, and the difficult decisions facing families who once believed this coastal paradise would be their forever home.

For retirees and longtime property owners, the crisis raises serious questions about retirement security, homeowners insurance, property values, and the hidden risks of coastal living in California.

Would you accept a government buyout and walk away from your dream home, or would you stay and fight to save it?

mcFa1ZWc7SM.transcript: Multi-million dollar oceanfront homes are being redtagged. Utilities are pulling the plug on entire streets. And the federal government is spending more than $54 million just to buy out houses and tear them down because the ground underneath them won't stop sliding. Stand on the edge of Palos Verda's Drive South at the curve above Portuguese Bend and look toward the water. What you see looks like paradise. Below you, the hillside drops toward the Pacific in long green terraces, tile roofs, glass walls, and swimming pools catching the afternoon sun. About 20 miles out across the water, Catalina Island sits on the horizon like a postcard. On this peninsula, Ocean View homes list for three, four, or $5 million. Just a few minutes up the hill in the gated town of Rolling Hills. Estates go on the market for close to $10 million. Yet, the price tag isn't what makes these houses shocking. The ground is. Look down at the road under your feet. The asphalt rolls like a frozen wave. There are patches stacked on top of patches. Crews don't repave this road once a decade. They repave it over and over because the road is never quite where it was last month. That's because the entire hillside is moving right now while you stand there. The latest survey from May of 2026 has the Portuguese Bend landslide moving about 1.21 in every week. That's roughly 5 in a month and more than 5t a year. Back in the summer of 2024, parts of this slope moved about 11 inches in a single week, almost a foot every seven days. This isn't a hairline crack in one driveway. The Greater Portuguese Bend Landslide Complex covers roughly 680 acres of coastline, which is more than 500 football fields of earth sliding toward the Pacific Ocean all at once. And this isn't some remote cliffside village tucked away from civilization. It's in Los Angeles County about 40 minutes from downtown on one of the most expensive peninsulas in America. When buyers moved in here, they thought they were getting two things you can't manufacture. A private permanent view of the Pacific and solid ground sitting underneath that view. Every single price on this hill assumed the hill would stay where it was. Today, the hill is not where it was. In July of 2024, the gas company shut off service to 135 homes here and gave no date for turning it back on. A few weeks later, the electric company cut the power. The governor of California declared a state of emergency. City inspectors went doortodoor and about 20 homes got red tags, meaning nobody is allowed to live inside. A glass chapel that had stood above this coast since 1951 was taken apart piece by piece and trucked away before the ground could tear it in half. And hanging over all of it is this. The city is now taking more than $54 million in federal money to buy these homes from their owners and knock them down. When you build multi-million dollar homes on a hill that's been sliding since 1956, the ground doesn't care how much you paid. This is the story of Portuguese Bend, one of the most beautiful, most expensive, and most unstable neighborhoods in America, and why the owners, the utilities, the city, and the state all can't stop it. To understand why Portuguese Bend is moving, you first have to understand what it was built on. Even more importantly, you have to understand when. The name goes back to the 1800s when Portuguese whalers worked this stretch of coast hunting grey whales as they passed the point. For most of its history, the whole peninsula was ranch land. In 1913, a New York banker named Frank Vanderlip bought roughly 16,000 acres of it and dreamed of turning it into a Mediterranean style resort on the Pacific. The real building came later. Around the Second World War, private beach communities went in along the shore. One was the Portuguese Bend Club and another was what became the Portuguese Bend Beach Club, complete with gates, a private beach, and houses close enough to the water to hear the waves at night. Up the slope, more homes followed, scattered across the terraces with that same view of Catalina. What none of those buyers could see was what lay 100 ft down. Geologists will tell you this entire slope is an ancient landslide. It isn't one that happened a few centuries ago. This hillside slid toward the ocean thousands of years before anyone ever built a house here, then settled and sat still. On the surface, it looked like solid ground with grass, trails, and gentle terraces. Underneath, it was really a giant block of broken earth resting on a slick surface, waiting for a reason to move again. In 1956, it got one. That summer, Los Angeles County was extending Crenshaw Boulevard south toward the top of the old slide. That road work put a heavy load of filled dirt right at the head of the landslide. In late August of 1956, the ground below began to move. It didn't collapse in one afternoon. It crept. Foundations cracked, walls leaned, and pipes snapped underground. Over the following months, the slide spread downhill toward the water. A news reel filmed in 1958 reported that around 140 of roughly 170 homes in the area had been destroyed or displaced. The homeowners sued the county and won. In 1961, a court awarded them roughly $10 million. Yet, the ground did not stop. It never has. From that summer of 1956 until today, the Portuguese Bend landslide has been moving every single year. Some years barely at all, and some years a lot. So, in 1978, the newly formed city of Rancho Palos Veres drew a line around the danger. It created what it calls a landslide moratorum area, a zone where building new homes is heavily restricted. Keep that year in your head. 1978 is going to matter at the very end of this story. The houses that were already there stayed. People kept living in them, buying them, and selling them. They loved them, and for decades, the movement was slow enough to live with. Then the weather changed. To understand what happened next, you have to understand how a landslide like this works because it's not what most people picture. The core Portuguese Ben slide covers about 260 acres. On average, the moving mass of earth is around 135 ft thick. Picture a slab of dirt and rock as tall as a 13-story building and as wide as a neighborhood resting on a sliding surface roughly 100 ft below the homes. That sliding surface contains layers of clay formed from ancient volcanic ash. When it's dry, that clay grips. When it's wet, it turns slick, almost like soap. So, friction holds a slope like this in place, and water destroys friction. Every gallon of rain that soaks into this hillside works its way down toward that clay layer. Every gallon of water that seeps out of the ground does the exact same thing. Whether it comes from a garden sprinkler, a leaking pipe, or a septic tank, and much of this area has long relied on septic systems. The more water collects down there, the higher the pressure, the weaker the grip, and the faster the slab above it slides. Then there's the other end of the hill. At the bottom, the landslide meets the Pacific Ocean. Waves hit the toe of the slide every day and carry away the dirt and rock that act like a doors stop at the base. Take away that doors stop and the slab above has less holding it back. So, the hill gets pushed from two directions at once with water lubricating it from above and the ocean undermining it from below. Sitting on top of all of it are hundreds of homes, a winding coastal road, water manes, gas lines, and power poles. None of it designed to move. For years, the city and local homeowners fought this with pumps. Around 1980, they drilled wells to pull groundwater out of the slide and keep that clay layer as dry as possible. It worked sort of. The movement slowed and the hill crept. People adjusted. They shimmed doors, re-leveled floors, and patched the road. That was the deal for decades. live on the hill, pay to keep it calm, and hope the weather cooperates. Then, in the winter of 2022 and 2023, the weather stopped cooperating. A parade of atmospheric river storms slammed Southern California. Rain fell in amounts this coast hadn't seen in years. That water soaked deep into the slope and reached the clay. By the spring of 2023, the slide had changed. It was no longer creeping. It was moving. The movement spread across the greater landslide complex. all those roughly 680 acres. Fresh cracks opened in streets that had been fine the year before. Homes began to tilt, water lines broke, and gas lines and power poles were pulled out of position. In October of 2023, the city declared a local emergency. Instead of drying out the next winter brought more rain in February of 2024, more storms hit the peninsula and the slide accelerated again. That same month, the Wayfar's Chapel, a church of glass and redwood designed by Lloyd Wright, son of Frank Lloyd Wright, closed its doors because the ground beneath it was moving. The chapel had stood above this coast since 1951 and was a national historic landmark. Over the following months, crews took it apart piece by piece, numbering the glass and timber so it could be rebuilt somewhere else, somewhere that doesn't move. By the summer of 2024, the measurements were staggering. Parts of the Portuguese Ben slide were moving about 11 in per week. That's nearly 4 feet a month. If it had kept that pace for a full year, some lots would have shifted more than 45 ft. Satellite radar data from NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory captured in the fall of 2024 showed sections of the peninsula still sliding as much as 4 in a week toward the ocean. Down at the Portuguese Ben Beach Club, the deformation was visible right from the sand. The road along the seaw wall buckled and the ground across the beach shifted by roughly four to five feet. When the ground moves that fast, it's not only the houses that are in trouble. Everything buried under them is too. In late July of 2024, residents got a notice from SoCal Gas, the region's gas utility. Its engineers had concluded that the gas system in Portuguese Bend could no longer be operated safely because the pipes were being stretched and bent by the moving ground. The notice came with about 3 days warning. Residents asked for a delay and so did the city. The utility said no. On July 29th, 2024, SoCal Gas shut off natural gas to about 135 homes in Portuguese Bend, giving no estimated date for restoring service. The company said it had detected no leaks and was acting before one could happen, giving each affected account holder $2500 to help with immediate needs. Think about what that means inside a house worth millions of dollars. No gas means no gas stove, no gas water heater and no gas furnace. Families bought electric hot plates and portable heaters. Some switched to propane tanks on their patios, and some just started taking cold showers. The next question in the neighborhood was obvious. If the gas lines couldn't take it, what about the power lines? Southern California Edison had already warned that it might have to act because its poles and wires were being dragged out of alignment by the same moving ground. Out here, a power line that snaps or sags into dry brush isn't just an outage. It's a wildfire risk on a hillside packed with homes. On Sunday, September 1st, 2024, Edison cut power to about 140 homes in the Portuguese Bend Beach Club and Portuguese Bend Club neighborhoods, calling the shut off indefinite. Evacuation warnings went out. The next day, it cut power to about 105 more homes in the nearby Sea View area. And for about 20 of those, the shut off was also indefinite. It happened right in the middle of a heatwave. Picture the daily routine in one of the most expensive zip codes in Los Angeles County. There's no gas and no electricity, so there's no air conditioning, no refrigerator, and no lights after sunset. The hum you hear at night comes from generators sitting on driveways and running on fuel that has to be hauled in. Some families packed up and left for hotels, rentals, or relatives guest rooms. Others stayed because leaving felt like giving up the house. Joe Badami is one of the ones who stayed. More than a year after the shut off, he told the Los Angeles Times he was running his home on rooftop solar panels and two big batteries and starting a generator whenever the batteries ran low. We're very careful, he said. We keep everything off. He had even had his house lifted to make up for the ground shifting underneath it. Most of the homeowners the paper interviewed had spent somewhere between $40,000 and $150,000 on generators, fuel, propane, solar, and electric conversions just to keep living in their own houses. 2 days after the power went out, Governor Gavin Newsome declared a state of emergency for Rancho Palos Verdees. The local emergency was now a state emergency, opening the door to more state resources and support. By then, the city had already started going doortodoor. Inspectors looked for signs that a home was was no longer safe. Doors that wouldn't close, floors that sloped, walls separating from foundations, and cracks in the structure itself. Homes considered dangerous got a red tag, meaning no one could live there. Others got yellow tags, which allowed limited use with restrictions. By 2025, about 20 homes in the landslide area carried red tags. Their owners still held the deeds, still owed property taxes, and still owned a house worth millions on paper. Yet, they were no longer allowed to sleep in it. So, who was supposed to stop this? The obvious answer is the people who own the houses. Those owners discovered something that surprises a lot of Americans. A standard homeowner's insurance policy does not cover earth movement. Fire. Yes. A burst pipe. Often, when the ground under your house slides, most policies treat that as a risk you took on when you bought the land. Special coverage for landslides is rare and expensive. And on a hill that's been moving since 1956, it's close to impossible to find. The next answer is the utilities. And they did act. Except what they did was shut things off, not save anything. Gas lines and power poles can be rerouted, raised, and replaced, but they can't be made to hold still on ground that's moving inches every week. From the utilities side, keeping service running was the danger, and cutting it was the safety measure. From the residents side, the cutoff made their homes almost impossible to live in. Both of those things are true at the same time. That leaves the city and the city did more than almost anyone expected. Rancho Palos Veres went back to the oldest weapon there is, pulling the water out. Crews drilled deep deatering wells into the slide to pump out the groundwater sitting on that slick clay layer. They lined cracks so rain would run off instead of soaking in. And they worked on drainage in the canyons above the slide so storm water would be carried away instead of seeping down into the hill. Each deep well can cost around $200,000 to build. The pumps run day and night, pulling water out on a massive scale. By the city's own count, its deep wells removed more than 370 million gallons of groundwater from the bottom of the Portuguese Ben slide within about a year. It worked, at least in part. The movement slowed through 2025. The slide averaged roughly 1.8 in a week, still nearly 8 feet a year, yet a fraction of the summer of 2024. Across most of the last two years, the average has hovered around 1.7 to 1.8 inches a week. By early 2025, some power had been restored in parts of the area. In late May of that year, SoCal Gas began bringing gas back to homes in nearby neighborhoods like Seeue, though it said the core Portuguese Bend community was still moving too much to reconnect, giving no timeline. Slowing a landslide isn't the same as stopping it. When the rain came back in early 2025, the slide sped up again to around 2 in per week. That fall, it dropped to about 1.46 in. And in May of 2026, after a winter with above average rainfall, the Portuguese bend slide was measured at about 1.21 in per week. That's about 5 in a month and more than 5 feet a year. Some areas on the western side of the complex are still moving 1 to 3 in a week. Now, look at what that effort costs. From October of 2022 through June of 2025, the city spent about $ 48 million on work in the landslide complex. Before the latest round of approvals, the city projected nearly $75 million in landslide related spending from 2022 through the middle of 2027. The city's general budget for running the whole city for a year with police contracts, parks, roads, and staff has been around $39 million. A small city has spent more than a year's worth of its budget trying to hold back a hillside, and the hillside is still moving. The state can declare emergencies, and the federal government can send grants. Yet, nobody with any amount of money can reach 100 ft down, grab a slab of earth hundreds of acres wide, and pin it in place. There's no wall big enough to hold it, and there's no pump that makes it stop. What you can do is slow it down, keep it from getting worse, and decide what to do about the people living on top of it. That is where the money started moving in a different direction. On October 28th, 2024, at a packed town hall, the city stood next to representatives from FEMA and the California Governor's Office of Emergency Services and announced a $42 million voluntary property buyout program for homeowners in the greater Portuguese Bend landslide area. The money came from FEMA's hazard mitigation grant program, and the city called it the largest grant in its history. The idea was simple. If you can't make the ground safe for the house, you remove the house from the ground. The city would buy qualifying homes at fair market value, not at today's value with red tags and gas shut offs. But based on appraisals from December 1st, 2022, before the slide accelerated, the program would pay what these homes were worth before the hill started moving fast. There was a catch. FEMA covers 75% of eligible costs and under the program's guidelines, a 25% cost share is generally deducted from what the homeowner receives. So, an owner who sells gets a check based on the pre- disaster value minus roughly a quarter. The deadlines were tight. Owners had about a week to request an inspection by November 4th and until November 8th to submit a full application. Then they waited. Federal buyouts don't move at the speed of a landslide. Each property requires appraisals, environmental reviews, title work, and federal approval. For nearly two years, while the ground kept moving underneath them, the owners who applied lived in limbo. Some were out of their homes, and some were in homes without full service. Most were still paying for houses they couldn't sell to anyone else. On October 14th, 2026, the answer finally came. FEMA awarded Rancho Palos Verdees more than $54 million in grants to buy 27 properties in the Portuguese Bend area in two rounds. Round one covers 22 homes, 16 of them red tagged and six yellow tagged. Round two covers five more. The homes were chosen based on safety risk, meaning red or yellow tags, loss of utility service, and how badly the ground had damaged them. On October 29th, the city held an orientation for the owners of those 27 homes. And in early November, the city council voted 5 to0 to accept the money. The full package came to nearly $56 million. About $52 million for buying the properties, almost $2 million for running the program, and almost $2 million more for permanent electrical infrastructure to keep the deep deatering wells running. There's also a third round waiting with the city applying for about $19 million more to buy around eight additional homes currently on a waiting list. So, the city is now very literally paying owners to leave. Yet, nobody has closed on a home yet, the city is preparing purchase offers and environmental assessments. And because federal money arrives as reimbursement, purchases will happen in small groups over the coming months. City staff have said that buying all 27 homes and demolishing them could take several years. Several years on ground, moving about 5 ft a year. Now, picture this from inside one of those houses. You bought a home with a view most people only see on postcards. You may have paid two, three, or more million dollars for it. It was the trophy, the house you plan to grow old in. Now there's a crack running across your living room floor. The sliding door to the patio doesn't line up with its frame anymore. The gas has been off. The power was off for a while, too, with the only light coming from a generator in the driveway. And there's a tag on your front door saying you can't live here. You can't sell to a normal buyer because who would buy it? On the open market, the numbers have already shifted. In the Portuguese Bend neighborhood, the median sale price recently fell about 17% in a single year. One house there was listed at just under $2 million, sat on the market for nearly a year, and finally sold for about 1.25 million, 37% below the asking price. The best way out on the table is the government buyout based on what your home was worth before the slide accelerated minus roughly a quarter paid out sometime in the next few months or next few years followed by your house getting knocked down. Even then, not everyone wants to take it. Some residents have told reporters they'd rather stay, pointing out that the wells are working, the slide has slowed, and they love the place and believe it can't be saved. Others have their names on the list and are counting the weeks. Sally Reeves is caught somewhere in between. She has lived in her ranchstyle house in Portuguese Bend since 1982. Today, a six-foot fisher splits her property. Her house is red tagged and propped up on wooden platforms, and she lives in a converted garage with most of her belongings in storage. She told Lace she applied for the buyout on the very last day, reluctantly, and she still hasn't decided whether she'll accept it. "We got snake bit, that's all," she said. While she waits on FEMA, she insists she's functioning just fine. On this hill, losing everything doesn't happen in a single day. It happens about an inch at a time. The tragedy of Portuguese Bend is that none of this was hidden. Geologists knew this was an ancient landslide. The county learned what happens when you disturb it in 1956 at the cost of about 140 homes. The city drew a moratorium map in 1978. The pumps have been running since around 1980. The ground has moved every single year for 70 years and still the homes stayed and the prices climbed. A peninsula with the best views in Los Angeles kept selling to as if the ground underneath was as permanent as the view. When it finally came due, every party involved ran into limits of its own. In 1956, a court case tied the slide to county road work. Today, scientists point to the rain. The utilities point to safety and the risk of fire and explosion. The city points to its budget already stretched far beyond what a town its size usually spends. The state and federal governments point to their grant programs, which by law take time, and all of them point to the weather, those backto-back wet winters that soaked the clay and woke the hill up. Every one of those limits is real, and none of them stops the ground. You can pay millions for a house on this coast. You can drill dozens of wells and pump hundreds of millions of gallons of water out of a hillside. You can line every crack, reroute every pipe, and patch every road. Yet, you cannot negotiate with a landslide. When you build a neighborhood on a slab of ancient earth resting on a layer of wet clay above the Pacific Ocean, the geology eventually catches up with you. Once the city buys a house, it gets demolished and the land is restored. Under FEMA's buyout rules, land acquired this way has to stay open space permanently with nothing new ever built on it. One lot at a time, the most expensive neighborhood on this coast starts turning back into open hillside. That brings us right back to 1978. The moratorium the city drew that year has limited new construction in the landslide zone for almost five decades. And now the city keeps debating how far those limits should go, whether anything should ever be rebuilt there again, and how much longer and at what cost it can keep pumping out the water that holds the hill back. For the people still there, the number that matters is about 1.2 inches a week, roughly 5 inches a month, and more than 5 feet a year. As of the city's latest survey, after the wells, the drains, and tens of millions of dollars, nobody can say what next winter's rain will do to it. Tonight, the sun will set over Catalina Island uh the way it always does. The view from the terraces will be just as beautiful as the day those homes were bought. The pumps will keep running in the dark, and the hill will keep moving. It isn't fast and it isn't dramatic. Yet, it doesn't stop. It has been moving since 1956.

COtyIqnTSJE.transcript: At 8:40 a.m. on September 16, 2026, a massive landslide struck Shi Daguan village in Mal County, Aba Perfecta, Shutan Province. Videos show yellow earth mixed with huge rocks pouring down from the mountain like a massive wave. Thick dust rose into the sky like a giant mushroom cloud. The enormous landslide carried trees and buildings down the slope, burying multiple structures and sections of the river channel below within seconds. The person filming repeatedly shouted, "Oh my god, oh my god, this is terrifying." According to a statement later released by the Ma County Emergency Management Bureau, the collapse occurred in the Ding Jibar area. The landslide completely cut off traffic on National Highway 213 in Ma County. More seriously, a huge amount of earth and rock rush into the Min River riverbed, causing one of the most important waterways in western Shutan to stop flowing. However, the official statement said the water from the upper Min River had already been diverted through a power station and there was temporarily no danger. According to Chinese media, because this unstable slope had already been identified during early inspections and placed under monitoring, local authorities have moved all 161 residents from the threatened area to safety before the disaster and provided temporary accommodation. A temporary traffic restriction was also put in place one day before the incident. Thanks to early warning and preventative measures, the landslide caused no casualties. The reason this massive landslide was detected in advance was that signs of geological movement had appeared at the site months earlier. In fact, since August, the Ding Jabar area had already experienced several small and medium-sized landslides. On September 8th, another larger landslide occurred, causing serious concern among local residents. In addition, sources familiar with the situation said that last month, geological survey workers and local residents discovered a huge crack at the top of the mountain measuring dozens of feet long and about 3 ft wide. In rock and soil mechanics, this indicates that the internal structure of the mountain has suffered a major rupture. A massive section of rock had become completely detached from the surrounding bedrock and was being held in place only by weak friction at the base of the slope. It was one of the most dangerous warning signs of an imminent largecale collapse. The recent continuous autumn rain flowed deep into the mountain through these cracks. It not only sharply increased the weight of the unstable slope, but also soaked and weakened the deeper sliding surface. Eventually, the force of the water destroy the remaining resistance, triggering this devastating mountain collapse. What's truly alarming is the blocked Ming River and the risk that the massive amount of debris could accumulate in the river channel and form a barrier lake. After the landslide, nearby villages and towns were again ordered to evacuate urgently. >> It's over. It's over. This whole area is going to be flooded. Everyone will have to leave. The river below has been completely blocked. The area upstream is going to be underwater. >> As one of the largest tributaries of the upper Yanzi River, the Ming River carries an enormous volume of water, creating immense hydraulic pressure and kinetic energy upstream. Once the river is blocked, the water level behind the landslide dam could rise rapidly, flooding upstream villages, farmlands, roads, and even water facilities. This echoed the fears of local residents at the scene. The whole area above will be flooded. However, a more dangerous threat lies downstream of the landslide dam. This natural barrier made of loose soil, rocks, and fallen trees has an extremely unstable structure. It can't withstand continuous water pressure and prolong soaking at all. Once upstream water exceeds the storage capacity of the barrier lake, causing water to overflow the dam or if largecale seepage occurs inside the dam due to piping. The fragile earth and rock dam could collapse suddenly. The flood released by a dam failure could be hundreds of times more destructive than a normal flood, carrying huge amounts of sediment and boulders. The burst flood could sweep downstream with devastating force. More seriously, the blockage of the Min River and the formation of a barrier lake directly threaten the downstream Zipingu reservoir and could pose a major challenge to the world famous Du Jang Yan irrigation system, a UNESCO World Heritage site. An insider at the Three Gorgeous Corporation said that if the river remains blocked for too long and the barrier lake reaches a dangerous water level, an uncontrollable dam collapse could send massive flood waters into the Diingp reservoir, creating an unpredictable impact on the safe operation of the dam. This domino effect triggered by a landslide could transform a localized geological disaster into a strategic crisis potentially affecting water security across the Chandu plane. Although the official statement briefly said that upstream water from the Min River has already been diverted through a power station and there is no danger, the existence of the barrier lake itself remains a major risk. Authorities also said that multiple departments were working through the night to discuss response measures. Dashi town in Ma County is located at the intersection of the Hunduan mountains where the Tibetan plateau transitions to the Shutan basin and the long menshan fault zone. The area has rugged terrain and highly active geological conditions. Historically, Dashi has been one of the areas most affected by earthquakes, landslides, mudslides, and other geological disasters. The most devastating event occurred in the Dashi earthquake in 1933. According to geological records, the magnitude 7.5 Dashi earthquake that year caused widespread mountain collapse and the large scale sinking of land. A total of about 196 million cubic yards of landslide debris blocked the Ming River, forming several barrier lakes, including what's now known as Dashi Haidu, the ancient city of Dashi, and over 3,000 soldiers and civilians were swallowed by flood waters. Within moments, the entire city sank beneath the lake. The earthquake and the later collapse of the barrier lakes caused over 20,000 casualties. 75 years later, the magnitude 8.0 Win earthquake in 2008 struck the same region again. Mal County located about 25 miles from Wrine County was also among the hardest hit areas. At the time, transportation, electricity, and communications in Mao County were completely cut off, leaving the county isolated from the outside world for nearly 46 hours. Highintensity seismic waves not only cause visible surface collapse but also inflicted structural damage deep inside the mountains. Geological engineering refers to this type of damage as earthquake fractured rock masses. Strong earthquakes send seismic waves repeatedly reflecting and interacting inside rock layers, opening existing fractures and creating large numbers of deep cracks. These cracks extending tens or even hundreds of feet underground break previously solid rock formations into loose fragments. This significantly reduces the rock masses cohesion, sheer strength, and internal friction, leaving long-term structural damage within the mountains. These deep cracks also provide channels for surface water and groundwater to seep in. When rainwater flows deep into the mountains through these fractures, the broken rock can easily lose its sheer strength after soaking and lubrication. After the combined impact of two major earthquakes, the stability of the mountains around Shaan village has continued to decline. Geological studies show that the postearquake effects of major earthquakes can last for decades with active periods typically continuing for 50 to 100 years. During this period, landslides and mudslides in earthquake affected areas occur more frequently than before the earthquakes. The most representative historical example of this post earthquake effect was the massive landslide that struck Shingmo village in the town in 2017. On June 24th, 2017, a high alitude long-d distanceance collapse occurred at Fuguay Mountain in Shing Mo Village, which also is in Ditown. About 10.5 million cubic yards of earth and rock suddenly collapsed from the mountain side and completely buried Shing Mo Village within just tens of seconds, leaving 141 people dead or missing from 62 households. The massive debris flow poured into the river and directly blocked about 1.2 miles of Song Ping, a tributary of the Ming River. Villagers from Leanga Cole village who witnessed the disaster described the scene. The ground shook violently followed by sparks that looked like electrical wires being energized. Thick clouds of dust rose into the air. The entire village disappeared moments later. In the northwest corner of Shing village, only one family of three escaped because they were changing diapers for their month old baby. Most villages were buried while still asleep. After the disaster, the site was covered with rocks and almost no trace of buildings remaining. After investigation, geological experts involved in rescue efforts and disaster assessments concluded that the disaster was a high altitude long distance collapse and landslide triggered by prolonged rainfall. Because the failure point was located at an elevation of over 11,000 ft in a remote high alitude area covered by dense vegetation, traditional geological surveys and high precision satellite remote sensing technologies were unable to detect the smallcale deformation of the slope in advance. Deep rock damage caused by historical earthquakes combined with accumulated rainfall was the main cause of the disaster. However, this explanation has been challenged by some experts. Chinese state media itself has previously highlighted that China has what it described as the world's most advanced and extensive satellite monitoring system for geological disasters. As early as the early 1980s, the former Ministry of Geology and Mineral Resources Geological Remote Sensing Center began using foreign satellite multi-spectral imagery to conduct geological disaster surveys in the Three Gorgees Reservoir area. Since 1999, the Aerospace Information Research Institute worked with the German research center for geosciences to conduct experimental deformation monitoring using insar technology on ancient landslide areas in the three gorgeous region including singan and the lean cliff. After 2007, as a new generation of highresolution SAR satellites and long wavelength radar satellites, technologies matured internationally, China accelerated related research in SAR technology was also applied to the national 973 program project. Research on disastercausing factors identification, precursor information, acquisition, and early warning methods for large landslides in western mountainous areas, producing significant results. Experts in geological disaster prevention and remote sensing surveying generally agree that remote sensing technology can help solve the problem of early identification of geological hazards. in particular in SAR technology can monitor slope deformation and changes before disasters. Shitran province has been designed as a key area for implementing these technologies. Therefore, whenever geological disasters cause casualties, the advanced geological disaster satellite monitoring systems promoted by the Chinese communist authorities often fail to play the role of protecting people's lives and property. The Shu Daguan village landslide occurring 9 years after the 2017 Shimo village landslide shares highly similar regional geological conditions with that disaster. Fortunately, this time in the Shuaguan village landslide showed clear warning signs beforehand preventing casualties. Another difference is that tunnel excavation was underway at the landslide site. According to Chinese media reports and on-site footage, the location where the landslide came to rest in Shagawagwan village, Ma County was close to the tunnel entrance and excavation face of the Truan Wan Expressway, which was under construction. The construction project office was located directly below the landslide area. This closed geographical overlap has led to questions over whether the tunnel construction was linked to the landslide. The Tranwen Expressway, officially known as the G0611 Tran Juul Wen Expressway, has a total planned length of 199 km. The project includes 51 bridges and 20 tunnels with bridges and tunnels accounting for 93.4% of the entire route. It has the highest bridge and tunnel ratio among expressway projects in Chuchan province exceeding 150 km in length. The Tranwen Expressway is being developed and constructed by the Shu Dal Group and is scheduled to open in 2030. The project has a total investment of 56.5 billion yen, about US 7.9 billion, with an average construction cost of 284 million yen, which is about $40 million per kilometer. This represents an extremely high budget for a four-lane expressway project in China. The main bridges of the Tronwin Expressway runs along the Min River Valley. Nearly 106 miles of the route runs parallel to the Min River and the Malwin seismic fault zones passing through areas affected by the Dei Son and Wentran earthquakes. In the Mau County section alone, the 54.3 mile route includes plans for seven extra long tunnels and three mega bridges. Although authorities haven't made any determination on whether the tunnel construction was related to the landslide, building large scale infrastructure in such fragile and continuously deforming geological formations carry a significant engineering risk. Engineering geology experts say that in high mountain canyon areas, tunnel construction can affect slope stability mainly through two mechanical processes. The first is the unloading effect. Rocks inside mountains are originally under a state of three-dimensional pressure balance. When tunnels are excavated at the base of a mountain, surrounding rock layers loose lateral support causing stress release. This can lead to outward loosening and cracking in the mountain above and around the tunnel. If a tunnel entrance is located at the base of a potential landslide area, excavation could disrupt the mountains mechanical balance. The second is blasting vibrations. In mountains already fractured by major earthquakes, repeated blasting waves can create resonance inside rock layers, causing small cracks previously closed or near failure to reopen and expand. These cracks may eventually connect and form sliding surfaces. Technical analysis suggest that the combined efforts of engineering blasting vibrations can accelerate instability in loose soil and fractured mountain formations. Some users pointed out that the Chinese Communist Party's years of excessive development of mountains and waterways without consideration of consequences are a major reason behind the increasing number of disasters today. Some users commented that this was similar to the mudslide in a pole. Repeated blasting during construction caused vibrations to build up, leaving the loose soil to collapse. This was a disaster caused by human actions. If tunnel excavation physically removes support from the base of a mountain, then the large scale construction of hydro power stations and reservoirs in canyon areas can disrupt the internal water balance of mountain slopes. Shortly before the landslide in Mao County, another major infrastructure project in Arba Perfecture also experienced a serious collapse. On the afternoon of November 11th, 2025, the Hongchi bridge, part of a road reconstruction project in the reservoir area of the Shang Jang Cole Hydropower Station on the Dau River in Maracan City, Aba Perfecta collapsed shortly after it was completed. The bridge was 0.47 47 mi long with a main span of 722 ft and main peers reaching 564 ft high. Less than a year after it opened to traffic, a landslide on the right bank pushed the approach bridge and part of the roaded downward, sending them into the Dumul Drew River below. The official statement briefly attributed the accident to slope cracks caused by a landslide. However, renowned water engineering expert Wangi Law argued that in a detailed analysis, the main cause of the Hongchi bridge collapse was a reservoir induced landslide triggered by water storage at the Shwangja Co reservoir. In his analysis, Wang Law explained the mechanics behind geological disasters caused by reservoirs. As the key upstream reservoir in the Dardu River hydropower development project, the Shwangja Cole reservoir has a dam height of 1,33 feet, making it the world's tallest dam. One of the project's less publicly discussed purpose is to raise water levels for the proposed western route of the south to north water transfer project. During the first phase of water storage in May 2025, the water level rose by more than 260 ft, causing river water to extensively soak the vulnerable lower sections of mountain slopes around the reservoir. The impact of reservoir storage on mountain stability can occur in multiple ways. First, prolong exposure to water can weaken easily weathered rocks, causing severe water absorption and softening while sharply reducing its sheer strength. More critically, major fluctuations in reservoir water levels can create high pore water pressure and outward hydraulic pressure inside mountain slopes. This powerful waterdriven force can destroy the mechanical balance of reservoir bank slopes. Local residents said that after the first phase of water storage, surrounding slopes had experienced multiple collapses. The bridge construction company's preliminary analysis also acknowledged that the collapse was related to geological changes caused by reservoir water level fluctuations built in and an area highly prone to geological disasters. The bridge project apparently failed to fully assess the long-term impact of reservoir storage on slope stability during design and construction. With insufficient protective measures, the structure was eventually damaged by a landslide involving about 3.9 million cubic yards of earth and rock. The collapse of the Hongchi bridge is a classic example of a hydraulic engineering project facing consequences after aggressively altering a fragile geological environment. Together with the landslide near the tunnel construction site in Ma County, it highlights a harsh reality. Largecale human engineering activities including hydropower projects and tunnel excavation can become major factors affecting geological stability in the high mountain and Kenyan regions of western Shichan under the CCP's hubristic slogan of man can conquer nature countless expressways extra long tunnels and massive dams have been planned and built on earthquake fault zones with fractured rock formations continuous mechanical disturbance accumulated blasting vibrations and Major fluctuations in reservoir water levels can all alter the weight balance of mountain slopes and internal water pressure, placing additional stress on fragile geological structures. If the CCP remains focused on the grand narrative of being an infrastructure powerhouse, ignores the warning signs of environmental damage and continues greedy development in these fragile areas, the collapse of barrier lakes and more severe geological disasters could become an unavoidable challenge for communities along these routes. 4MCcfjm4eWA.transcript: On September 1st, several mainland Chinese internet users posted a video showing a landslide at Tiger Leaping Gorge. The footage showed rocks tumbling down the mountainside. The scenic area was nearby and tourists rushed to avoid the falling debris. The users who posted the video said the landslide occurred at around 2:30 p.m. and lasted for about 4 minutes. Fortunately, no casualties have been reported so far. According to online posts, rock falls had already occurred location on July 30th and in mid-August. With the latest incident, the area has now experienced three similar events in the same spot. On the afternoon of September 1st, the staff at the Gorge scenic area confirmed that a collapse had occurred that day, but said it was outside the official scenic area. They said the site remains open as usual. Officials from Tiger Leaping Gorge town said frequent rainfall in recent days may have loosened the soil and rocks contributing to the collapse. Online commenters wrote, "This is extremely dangerous. Why are landslides happening so often here? Something serious will happen here sooner or later." Public information shows that Tiger Leaping Gorge is a famous canyon along the Jinsha River, the upper section of the Yangtze. It is located on the border between Lijiang City, Yunnan Province, and Shangri-La City in Tibet. The canyon has an elevation difference of more than 9,800 feet from the river bed to the mountain peaks. At its narrowest point, it is only about 100 feet wide, making it one of the deepest and most dangerous canyons in the world. Previously, a Chinese media reported that on July 18th, heavy rainfall flooded in the scenic area. Some buildings collapsed, walkways were flooded, and some tourists were trapped inside tunnels for nearly 2 hours. The construction and operation of hydropower projects can alter local geological and hydrological conditions, potentially triggering or worsening landslides. Notably, Chinese authorities have built, are building, or are planning to build numerous large hydropower stations in the area. In recent years, the entire Jinsha River has been almost filled with hydropower projects. In 2024, Chinese geologist and environmental scholar Fan Xiao published an article revealing that 27 cascade hydropower stations were planned along the mainstream of the Jinsha River from Yibin, Sichuan Province through Qinghai Province. The plan would completely transform the natural river into a chain of interconnected reservoirs. Currently, 12 hydropower stations along the middle and lower reaches of the Jinsha have been completed. Of the 13 planned stations on the upper Jinsha River, the Suwalong hydropower station has been completed, while six others are still under construction. Among them is the Xiluodu hydropower station on the mainstream of the Jinsha, upstream from Tiger Leaping Gorge and near the border of Sichuan Province and Yunnan Province. According to official statements, in August 2025, the project completed construction of the first inclined shaft of what was described as the steepest water diversion tunnel currently under construction in China. The main construction phase has now moved from excavation to concrete pouring. Fan Xiao has long studied and publicly criticized excessive hydropower development and water projects in western China, including cascade hydropower development and large dams along the Dadu River, Jinsha River, and the Three Gorges project. He cited their potential negative impacts on geological stability and the ecological environment. The proposed Tiger Leaping Gorge hydropower project, located in the upper section of the middle reaches of the Jinsha River, has attracted strong interest from hydropower developers because of its massive reservoir regulation capacity. Although its installed capacity is smaller than the Three Gorges Dam, the project has major advantages in reservoir storage and multi-year water regulation. Its water storage capability is even greater than that of the Three Gorges Dam. It is considered a multi-year regulating reservoir with a total storage capacity of about 48.5 billion cubic yards. However, Fan Xiao pointed out four major problems. First, the project is built on an active fault zone with intense geological activity, creating major risks of earthquakes, landslides, and other geological disasters. Second, it would damage natural landscapes, ecosystems, and cultural heritage sites, including Tiger Leaping Gorge and the First Bend of the Yangtze River at Shigu. These are part of the Three Parallel Rivers World Natural Heritage Site, National Scenic Areas, and Natural Protected Areas. Third, it would submerge roughly 33,000 acres of fertile farmland, villages, and rural areas in the Jinsha River Valley between Tongpan and Tachong, forcing at least 150,000 people to relocate and endanger their livelihoods. Fourth, the project harms the environment and sustainable development. Under the leadership of Hu Jintao and Wen Jiabao, Chinese authorities took a more cautious approach toward major water projects. Since 2004, the project faced strong opposition from Chinese citizens and international environmental organizations, and was suspended by 2007. Hydropower developers later renamed the hydropower station as the Longpan hydropower station in an attempt to restart the project. The Associated Press reported at the time that Hu Jintao avoided attending the completion ceremony of the highly controversial Three Gorges Dam. The report said Hu's decision was very different from previous CCP leaders, who often sought to associate themselves with major economic achievements. In September 2007, Chinese state media began reporting that officials had acknowledged various problems with the Three Gorges Dam. The Guardian reported at the time that then Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao had intervened to stop plans to build 13 dams and hydropower stations along the Nu River, calling the plan unscientific. Wen Jiabao had a background in geology. Earlier in his career, he spent 18 years working at the grassroots level in geological exploration and related work at the Gansu Provincial Bureau of Geology. However, after Xi Jinping came to power, many major water projects that had previously been blocked were restarted openly. In 2022, China's National Development and Reform Commission and National Energy Administration officially included the Longpan Hydropower Station, formerly known as the Tiger Leaping Gorge Hydropower Station, in major projects listed under the country's 14th renewable energy plan. At the national strategic level, the Longpan project was redefined as a major project for Yangtze River flood control and energy transition. The project was effectively revived. In 2024, the Longpan project began preparations for resettlement. At the end of 2025, Yunnan Huadian Longpan Hydropower Development Company was officially created specifically to oversee construction of the project. China affairs expert Yang Bo said that this shows that during the Hu Wen's era, authorities still showed some consideration for people's welfare, while under Xi Jinping, large-scale projects driven by ambition have ignored public interests. He said Xi reportedly claims people first, life first, but the launch of harmful projects like this reveals a pattern of making favorable statements while also pursuing damaging policies. After the 2008 Wenchuan earthquake, Fan Xiao also published research analyzing the potential impact of water storage and pressure infiltration from the Zipingpu reservoir on accelerating fault zone fractures and triggering earthquakes. He listed seven indicators used by Chinese researchers to assess reservoir-induced earthquakes, including a dam and reservoir reaching a certain scale, active faults in the reservoir area, significant recent tectonic movement, abnormal deep gravitational gradients, highly permeable rock formations, and previous earthquake activity. Fan Xiao said the Zipingpu reservoir met the first six of these criteria, indicating a high risk of triggering earthquakes. Fan pointed out that the reservoir has a dam height of 156 m and a water depth of more than 330 ft. The enormous weight of the stored water placed additional pressure on the Longmen Shan fault zone. At the same time, water seeping deep into the ground effectively acted as a lubricant, reducing the fault zone's resistance to shearing and accelerating the fracturing process. China has seen repeated natural disasters and man-made disasters with landslides occurring frequently in recent months. Affected by heavy rainfall brought by Typhoon Saudel, flash floods struck parts of Beihu District in Changde Hunan Province. On August 21st, more than 10 landslides occurred while more than 20 road sections were blocked by collapses. Chinese authorities emphasized rescue operations and claimed that as of September 1st, there were zero deaths and no missing people. However, some observers questioned whether the full extent of the disaster had been disclosed. On the early morning of August 23rd, Fengshan Town in Yunnan Province was hit by prolonged heavy rainfall. A mudslide struck Anshu Village while a landslide occurred at Shriching Village. As of 5:00 p.m. that day, the disaster had left two people dead and four others missing. Videos from the scene showed mudslides carrying large amounts of trees and rocks into the village. Some roads were destroyed while mud and debris piled up around homes. Firefighters carried out search and rescue operations at collapsed mountain areas and among the ruins. At around 8:00 a.m. on August 15th, a landslide occurred in Pingnan County, Guangxi Province. Large numbers of trees were swept down with the mud and soil. During the incident, an elderly man carrying an umbrella happened to walk through the area. As trees repeatedly fell toward him, he quickly dodged the falling debris. Fortunately, he escaped the series of impacts. On July 20th, a landslide and collapse occurred in Qinglong County, Guizhou Province, destroying multiple roads and leaving more than half of one roadway missing. On the morning of July 17th, a major mountain collapse occurred near the Wujiang River in the Miao and Tujia Autonomous County, Chongqing. The disaster killed 51 people, left 10 missing, and injured 10 others. On July 13th, continuous rain and wind brought by a typhoon triggered a landslide near Gua'ao Village near Yueqing, Zhejiang Province. Large rocks fell into the road, forcing a nearby bus stop to suspend service. Workers used excavators to clear the fallen rocks. A local villager commented under CCTV video saying the road is the only route villagers use to enter and leave the area every day. The person said small rocks had already been falling from the mountain about a month earlier. Villagers had reported the issue to village and township authorities and repeatedly called the government hotline. However, the relevant departments only installed a simple protective barrier and failed to take any substantial reinforcement or hazard removal measures. The commenter said ordinary barriers could not withstand large-scale rockfalls during heavy rain and typhoon conditions and urged authorities to address the danger at its source. Shortly afterward, the critical comment was reportedly removed by online censors. On June 23rd, a section of the Tongchuan Bridge in Liuzhou, Guangxi Province was hit by flash floods. The bridge foundation and supports were left exposed after the surrounding soil was washed away. The most devastating disaster in recent months was the massive flash flood and landslide disaster along the China-Nepal border in late August whose impacts continue to be felt. The catastrophic landslide that struck the border on August 26th severely affected areas near Tibet's Shigaste City and Rasuwa District in Nepal. So far, more than 1,000 people in the two countries have died and more than 4,500 people remain missing. Videos from the Nepalese side of the disaster showed a large section of the mountain slope suddenly collapsing in a canyon. Large amounts of rock and soil poured down the mountainside, quickly creating a massive cloud of dust that covered the road and valley below. A person filming from the opposite mountain side captured the entire process from the initial collapse to the massive landslide. As the collapse continued, grayish yellow dust spread through the valley, almost completely blocking the view of the entire canyon. Regarding the cause of the mudslide, Chinese experts have generally said the main trigger was the collapse of a glacier inside Nepal. They said the glacier broke apart, triggering a rock collapse and all the broken material combined to form a glacial mudslide. However, this explanation differs significantly from analysis recently published by international researchers. Geologist Kristen Cook from the University of Grenoble in the Alps, and a member of the Nepal mudslide investigation team, recently published her analysis in National Geographic, saying that the disaster was caused by the sudden collapse of bedrock beneath the glacier. The collapse dragged the entire glacier down the mountain slope. The rapidly falling ice melted quickly and blocked the river, eventually causing a deadly outburst from a landslide dammed lake. In an interview with Radio France International, Kristen Cook explained that the glacier itself did not contain nearly enough energy to melt such a large amount of ice. If only a glacier were involved, it would more likely have resulted in an ice avalanche. An ice avalanche would move slowly down the valley and would not develop into such a massive flood. A huge amount of rock was needed to trigger an event of this scale and to generate enough heat to melt the ice. Glacier collapses are closely linked to glacial activity, while rock collapses are largely determined by geological conditions and geological history. The driving forces behind glacier collapses and rock collapses are different. Independent commentator Taishen Kun wrote that the disaster along the China-Nepal border involved not only natural forces, but also human factors. He said the large-scale infrastructure development in the Himalayas has already damaged glaciers and high-altitude ecosystems, and this may only be the beginning. Without stopping and reassessing these projects, even larger and more frequent disasters could occur in the future. He wrote that the Himalayan region is already one of the world's most fragile ecosystems, and one of the areas most sensitive to climate change. Glacier retreat, permafrost melting, and expanding glacial lakes, combined with large-scale construction of roads, hydropower projects, mines, and tourism facilities have placed additional pressure on unstable mountains and valleys. A single extreme rainfall event, glacial lake outburst, or landslide could quickly intensify along river valleys, and eventually become a disaster affecting multiple regions, or even crossing national borders. Deputy Secretary General of the Taiwan Society of International Law, Lin Ting-Hui, criticized China's construction of dams, roads, and tunnels. Lin said that blasting mountains has damaged local ecosystems and geological stability. Combined with accelerating glacial melt, meltwater can seep into weakened slopes, and when heavy rainfall occurs, the scale and destructive power of mudslides can increase dramatically. As early as 2018, a Tibetan writer living in exile warned that China's large-scale construction of reservoirs and hydropower stations in Tibet, along with intensive mining activities, had become a time bomb for Tibetans. Water resources expert Wangwei Lo, who lives in Germany, said scientific reports had long warned that similar risks could occur again. He said if China had shared data earlier, downstream losses could have been reduced. In his view, the disaster was caused by a combination of ice and rock collapse, and human alteration of the terrain. Wangwei Lo pointed out that at the location where the two plateau rivers meet, in Kyirong, Tibet, construction projects have narrowed the river channel. This means that when massive amounts of mud and debris rush downstream at high speed, the floodwaters and debris the flows that would normally spread outward are forced into a much narrower channel. He said, "The narrower the river channel, the higher the mudslide can rise and the greater the impact on surrounding infrastructure. He also warned that the massive hydropower project on the Yarlung Tsangpo River faces similar high-altitude geological risks. The Yarlung Tsangpo mega hydropower project is located in Nyingchi City, Tibet. It plans to build five cascade hydropower stations with a total investment of about 1.2 trillion yuan, about 170 billion US dollars. The project is expected to have an installed of 70 million to 81 million kilowatts, equivalent to about three Three Gorges Dam projects. The mega project officially entered the construction phase after a groundbreaking ceremony was held in July 2025. Wang Weilo said, "The chain disasters involving high-altitude ice and rock collapses, landslide-dammed lakes, and mudslides are not rare in the Tibetan Plateau. Climate warming is making glaciers increasingly unstable. He warned that if the Yarlung Tsangpo mega project were to encounter a similar disaster, the risks and consequences would be far more severe." He added that the lack of widespread public opposition inside China is itself one of his biggest concerns. >> [music] [music]

muWG-Qf3l10.transcript: প্রাকৃতিক দুর্যোগের যেন এক ট্র্যাজিক কেন্দ্রস্থলে পরিণত হয়েছে হিমালয় কন্যা নেপাল। 2015 সালের ভূমিকম্পের পর এবারের আকশ্বিক বন্যা দেশটির অন্যতম ভয়াবহ প্রাকৃতিক বিপর্যয় হিসেবে বিবেচনা করা হচ্ছে। 1934 সালের রেকর্ড 8.1 মাত্রার প্রবল শক্তিশালী ভূমিকম্প থেকে 1993 সালে ভয়াবহ ক্লাউডওয়ার্স এসবই সহ্য করতে হয়েছে দেশটিকে। এমন প্রলয়নকারী প্রাকৃতিক দুর্যোগ মোকাবেলা করেই যেন টিকে থাকতে হচ্ছে হিমালয় কন্যা নেপালকে। দেশটির এমন বিপর্যয়কর পরিস্থিতির ইতিহাসটা বেশ লম্বা। ভূমিকম্প, ভয়াবহ ভূমিধষ ও আকশ্বিক বন্যা কোন কিছুই পিছু ছাড়ছে না দেশটির। 1938 সালের রেকর্ড 8.1 একমাত্রার প্রবল শক্তিশালী ভূমিকম্পে লন্ডভন্ড হয়ে গিয়েছিল নেপাল বিহার পুরো অঞ্চল যাতে প্রাণ হারিয়েছিলেন 100 হাজারের বেশি মানুষ এরপর 1988 সালে 6.9 মাত্রার ভূমিকম্পে নেপালে প্রাণ যায় 721 জনের। 1993 সালে কুলেখানি এলাকায় ভয়াবহ ক্লাউডবার্স থেকে সৃষ্ট বন্যা ও ধসে 1336 জন প্রাণ হারান। তবে আধুনিক নেপালের ইতিহাসে সবচেয়ে বড় ক্ষতটি তৈরি হয় 2015 সালের 25 এপ্রিল প্রায় 7.8 মাত্রার ধ্বংসাত্মক গোরখা ভূমিকম্পে প্রাণ হারান প্রায় 9000 মানুষ। ধষে পড়ে 10 লাখের বেশি ঘরবাড়ি। দুর্যোগের এই ধারা সাম্প্রতিক বছরগুলোতেও থেমে নেই। 2023 সালের 3 নভেম্বর পশ্চিম নেপালের জাজারকোট ও রুকুমে 5.6 মাত্রার ভূমিকম্পে মারা যায় দেশটির দেড় শতাধিক মানুষ। এর প্রায় এক বছর পর 2024 সালের সেপ্টেম্বরের দীর্ঘস্থায়ী বর্ষণ ও বন্যায় দেশ জুড়ে অন্তত 66 জনের মৃত্যু হয়েছিল বলে জানায় নেপাল সরকার। ইসহাদুল মাহমুদ, স্টার নিউজ।

zE9N4-UoP_E.transcript: কোন আগাম আভাস নেই। নেই ভূমিকম্পের তীব্র ঝাকুনি। অথচ চোখের সামনে আচমকায় ধপাস করে তলিয়ে গেল আস্ত একটি সড়ক। পাহাড় ধষসের ঘটনা আমাদের চেনা হলেও সমতলের বুকে এমন আকর্ষিক ধষ জন্ম দিচ্ছে নানা ভীতিকর প্রশ্নের। হঠাৎ কেন এই ভূমিধস? মাটির গভীরে ঠিক কি এমন ঘটছে যা আমাদের পায়ের তলার চেনা জমিনকে এভাবে নড়বরে আর অনিরাপদ করে তুলছে? এমনি এক অবিশ্বাস্য ও রুদ্ধশ্বাস ঘটনা ঘটেছে রাজধানীর মোহাম্মদপুরের মোহাম্মদিয়া হাউসিং সোসাইটির পাঁচ নম্বর রোডে। সেখানে সড়কের পাশে থাকা একটি পুরো দোকান মুহূর্তের মধ্যে আস্ত মাটির নিচে বিলীন হয়ে গেছে। ধষে পড়া স্থানটি প্রায় 40 ফুট গভীরে ডেবে যায় এবং দোকানের সমস্ত মালামাল মাটির অতলে চাপা পড়ে ধ্বংসস্তূপে পরিণত হয়েছে। তবে নিশ্চিত মৃত্যুর মুখ থেকে অলৌকিকভাবে বেঁচে গেছেন ওই দোকানের মালিক। অনুসন্ধানে জানা যায় গত রবি ও সোমবার রাতে ওই এলাকায় একটানা ভারী বৃষ্টিপাত হয়। মূলত এই বৃষ্টির জল জমে চারপাশের মাটি অতিরিক্ত নরম হয়ে যাওয়ার পরেই ঘটে এই ভয়াবহ ধষ। তবে স্থানীয়দের অভিযোগ সেখানকার পাঁচ নম্বর রোডে একটি আবাসন কোম্পানির নির্মাণাধীন ভবনের জন্য গভীর গর্ত খুরে পাইলিংয়ের কাজ চলছিল। কিন্তু পাইলিং এর ত্রুটির কারণে মাটির নিচে এক বিশাল শূন্যতার সৃষ্টি হয়েছিল। যা এই ভারী বৃষ্টিতে ধষে পড়ে। এই ঘটনায় স্থানীয় বাসিন্দারা চরম আতঙ্ক ও ক্ষোবে ফেটে পড়েছেন। ধসের ফলে চারপাশের বহুতল আবাসিক ভবনগুলো এখন প্রচন্ড ঝুঁকির মুখে পড়েছে। যেকোনো মুহূর্তে বড় ধরনের দুর্ঘটনার আশঙ্কায় আতঙ্কিত বাসিন্দারা অনেকেই নিজেদের ঘরবাড়ি ও ফ্ল্যাট ছেড়ে জিনিসপত্র নিয়ে নিরাপদ আশ্রয়ে সরে যাচ্ছেন। ঢাকা উত্তর সিটি কর্পোরেশন ইতিমধ্যেই ঘটনাস্থল পরিদর্শন করে সংশ্লিষ্ট কোম্পানির বিরুদ্ধে আইনি ব্যবস্থা ও জরিমানার প্রক্রিয়া শুরু করেছে। ফারহানা হক, এটিএন বাংলা।

shekMbjHcfA.transcript: আসসালামু আলাইকুম। কিছুক্ষণ আগে নেপালের একটি ভিডিও দেখলাম। পাহাড়ি বন্যা এবং পাহাড়ি ধস একটা দেশের কি বিপর্যয় আনতে পারে এটা এই ভিডিওটা যারা দেখেছেন তারা বলতে [মিউজিক] পারবেন। আমি আমার জীবনে এরকম ভিডিও আগে কখনো দেখিনি। বন্যা, জলোচ্ছাস, পাহাড়ধষ এমন হতে পারে এটা কল্পনাওতেও ছিল না। এই [মিউজিক] ভিডিওটা দেখে একটা বিষয় আপনাদের সামনে উপস্থাপন না করে পারছি না। আমি আসলে ভিডিও তৈরি করি না। তারপরেও মনে হলো বিষয়গুলি আসলে বলা দরকার। ভিডিওতে দেখতে পাচ্ছেন আপনারা মানুষ [মিউজিক] দৌড়াচ্ছে এবং পাহাড় থেকে ঢল নেমে আসছে নিচের [মিউজিক] বসৎবাড়ির দিকে। সুউচ্চ প্রাসাদ এবং পরিকল্পিত শহর। তার কোন কিছুর ছিটফোটাই এই বন্যার পরে আর দেখা যায়নি। এখনো পর্যন্ত প্রায় 400রও উপরে পর্যটক নিখোঁজ রয়েছে। [মিউজিক] ঘটনাটি ঘটেছে নেপালের একটি প্রদেশে যেটি চীনা সীমান্তের কাছাকাছি। যে বিষয়টি আমি আপনাদেরকে বলব যে দৃশ্য আমি দেখেছি এখানে। মানুষ দিক-বিদিক ছোটাছুটি করছে। তারা দেখতে পাচ্ছে যে জলসচ্ছাস অর্থাৎ বড় বড় ঢেউ এগুলি তাদের দিকে ধেয়ে আসছে। [মিউজিক] পানির প্রবাহ তাদের দিকে ধেয়ে আসছে। পাহাড় ধোষে তাদের দিকে ধেয়ে আসছে। মানুষ প্রাণপনে ছুটছে যার যার জীবন বাঁচাতে। [মিউজিক] কিন্তু একটা সময় এসে দেখা গেল মানুষ নিজেকে [মিউজিক] বাঁচাতে না পেরে এই প্রলয়নকরী ভূমিধষে বিলীন হয়ে গেল। চোখের সামনে ভিডিওগুলি দেখছিলাম। আর ওই কথাগুলি মনে পড়ছিল [মিউজিক] কেয়ামতের পূর্বে আল্লাহ রাব্বুল আলামীন বলেছেন পাহাড়গুলিকে ধষিয়ে দেওয়া হবে। পাহাড়গুলি তুলার মত উড়তে থাকবে। যদিও এটার সাথে আমি ইসলামের [মিউজিক] কোন কিছু মিলাচ্ছি না। তবে আমার দৃষ্টিভঙ্গি থেকে এটাই মনে হলো কেয়ামতের পূর্বে কি ঘটনা ঘটতে পারে, কেমন হতে পারে, মানুষ কিভাবে তার নিজেকে বাঁচানোর জন্য আপ্রাণ চেষ্টা [মিউজিক] করতে পারে। যদিও মুমিন ব্যক্তি যারা তারা তো আর কেয়ামত দেখবে না। কেয়ামতের পূর্বেই একটি ঠান্ডা বাতাস প্রবাহিত হবে এবং মুমিন বান্দা যারা রয়েছেন তারা দুনিয়া থেকে বিদায় নিবেন। এর পরবর্তীতে যারা বদকার থাকবেন অথবা যারা আল্লাহর আইনকে অমান্য করেন অথবা আল্লাহ তাআলাকে অমান্য করেন তাদেরকে [মিউজিক] এই কেয়ামত উপলব্ধি করাবেন আল্লাহ রাব্বুল আলামীন। প্রথমে দেখলাম একটা ছোট্ট পানির ফোয়ারা আসছে একটা নদীর মধ্য দিয়ে। [মিউজিক] আস্তে আস্তে সেটি বাড়তে থাকলো। ঘরবাড়ি ডুবে যেতে থাকলো। একটা ব্রিজের নিচ দিয়ে প্রথমে এটে যাচ্ছিল। পরবর্তীতে দেখলাম ব্রিজটাই হচ্ছে ভেঙে পানিতে ভেসে গেল। এবং এর পরবর্তীতে আস্তে আস্তে করে বাড়ি ঘর এবং বড় বড় বিল্ডিংগুলি কিভাবে ধসে গেল। প্রাকৃতিক এই বিষয়গুলি আমরা হয়তো কয়েকদিন পরেই ভুলে যাব। তবে একটা জিনিস চিন্তা করে দেখুন তো যদি এরকম কোন ঘটনা আপনার [মিউজিক] সাথে বা আমার সাথে ঘটতো আমরা কি এই ট্রামা থেকে বের হতে পারতাম কখনোই [মিউজিক] না এজন্যই বলি আল্লাহ রাব্বুল আলামীনের কাছে ফিরে আসি এবং তার দরবারে করুণা কামনা করি আল্লাহ রাব্বুল [মিউজিক] আলামীন এই দুর্যোগে যারা পড়েছেন এবং এই দুর্যোগ থেকে যারা মোকাবেলার চেষ্টা করছেন তাদেরকে হেফাজত করুন সে যে ধর্মের হোক যে বর্ণের হোক যে জাতির হোক যে গোষ্ঠীর হোক এবং
